---
title: "Assignment 5 — Quasi-harmonic thermodynamics of MgO"
---

Laboratory 5 brings together almost everything developed in the previous
activities. You will not run the underlying CRYSTAL phonon calculations during
the laboratory: a validated multi-volume dataset is provided because the
$4\times4\times4$ phonon calculations are too expensive for a teaching
session.

Your task is instead to understand **what was calculated, why those calculations
are needed, and how they become finite-temperature and finite-pressure
properties**.

Before starting, read **Laboratory 5 — From harmonic phonons to
finite-temperature properties**.

## Scientific questions

The laboratory is organized around four questions:

1. Why does a quasi-harmonic calculation require phonons at several volumes,
   including **expanded** volumes?
2. How does the choice of free-energy minimization — polynomial or equation of
   state — affect the derived properties?
3. Which calculated quantities can be compared directly with experiment, and
   under which thermodynamic conditions?
4. What can we learn when calculated and experimental **absolute values** differ
   but their **trends** agree?

## The supplied calculation series

The instructor provides seven CRYSTAL phonon calculations spanning

$$
V/V_\mathrm{ref}
=
0.91,\;0.94,\;0.97,\;1.00,\;1.03,\;1.06,\;1.09.
$$

Do not treat these files as a black box. The first notebook asks you to inspect
the input and output files and identify, among other things:

- the phonon supercell;
- the number of atoms in that supercell;
- the number of q-points sampled;
- the DFT functional and basis set;
- the sampled volume interval.

A central point of the assignment is to explain why the series must extend to
$V>V_\mathrm{ref}$. *Hint*: think about what happensby heating a material.

## Quasi-harmonic analysis

You will use Quantas to build a normalized multi-volume phonon input, inspect
its pressure coverage, and calculate quasi-harmonic properties.

Two representations of the free-energy curve will be compared using exactly
the same first-principles dataset:

```text
polynomial minimization
versus
BM3 equation-of-state minimization
```

The objective is not to decide that one method is universally "better". You
will examine which physical quantities are sensitive to the numerical
representation and whether both methods lead to the same scientific
interpretation.

## Comparison with experiment

The workspace includes documented experimental/reference data for MgO. You will
compare calculations with:

- standard entropy $S(T)$;
- constant-pressure heat capacity $C_P(T)$;
- enthalpy increment $H(T)-H(298.15\,\mathrm K)$;
- cell volume and thermal expansion at ambient pressure;
- adiabatic bulk modulus $K_S(T)$;
- room-temperature compression $V(P)$.

Experimental/reference points are plotted in **black** so that they remain
visually distinct from the different computational models.

Particular attention should be paid to two volume plots:

1. the **absolute** cell volume $V(T)$;
2. the **normalized** volume $V(T)/V(T_\mathrm{ref})$.

You will look for any systematic offset between theory and experiments, but also
check if the calculated trends agree with the reference data.

## Final interpretation

At the end of the laboratory you should be able to distinguish:

```text
numerical representation error
        from
first-principles model error
        from
limits of the QHA itself
```

Do not judge the calculation by the number of matching decimal places. The
scientific objective is to decide which **behaviours, derivatives and trends**
are reproduced and why.

Your completed notebooks constitute the assignment. Save, commit and sync your
work using the standard course workflow.
